Cite

SITE — sounds exactly like 'site' and 'sight,' but means to quote or reference, not a place or vision. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To cite to quote a passage or refer to something as evidence.

The lawyer was careful to cite the exact page number of the law she was relying on.

Worked Example

A journalist writes an article claiming a new law will raise taxes. To back up the claim, she quotes the exact section of the law and names the government website where readers can check it themselves.

Pointing directly to the exact source that backs up a claim is exactly what it means to cite something. Unlike 'mention,' which is casual, to cite specifically means referencing something as proof or evidence.

How Cite Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

quote

quote: to repeat someone's exact words

reference

reference: to mention as a source of information

invoke

invoke: to refer to something as support for an argument

Antonyms

omit

omit: to leave out or fail to include

ignore

ignore: to pay no attention to something

How Strong Is It? — mention → cite → document

mention vs. cite

mention vs. cite: Mention is weaker than cite — mentioning something is casual, while citing means formally pointing to it as evidence or proof.

document vs. cite

document vs. cite: Document is stronger than cite in a sense: citing points to an existing source as support, but documenting means creating a full, detailed record of evidence yourself.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — cite

root — cite: to call, to set in motion (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin citare ('to summon, to call') comes from ciere, meaning 'to set in motion.' To cite something is to formally 'call it forward' as evidence in support of a claim.

Use the root in a new word: excite

Use the root in a new word: excite: The surprise announcement was enough to excite the entire classroom into cheering.
